title: Ergonomics and Safe Lifting
standard: General Duty Clause, OSH Act Section 5(a)(1)
standard_title: Ergonomic hazards and musculoskeletal disorders (General Duty Clause; NIOSH lifting guidance)
summary: Sprains, strains and back injuries are among the most common and most costly injuries in public works, and most of them build up from ordinary lifting, shoveling, driving and tool use. This course covers how musculoskeletal disorders happen, the risk factors that stack up on a route or a job site, how to lift and move loads safely, when to reach for a cart or a hoist instead of your back, and why reporting an ache early keeps it from becoming surgery.
objectives: Recognize the common musculoskeletal disorders and the seven risk factors that cause them.
Explain how OSHA enforces ergonomic hazards under the General Duty Clause and what the NIOSH 51-pound limit means in practice.
Demonstrate the safe lifting steps from planning the lift to setting the load down, and know when a lift needs two people or a machine.
Choose the mechanical aid, tool and work method that takes the load off the body for common field and shop tasks.
Apply ergonomic practices in vehicles and equipment, including seat setup and three-point mounting and dismounting.
Report early signs of discomfort and use warm-up, microbreaks and job rotation to reduce exposure.

sections.heading: What musculoskeletal disorders are
sections.body:
A **musculoskeletal disorder (MSD)** is an injury to the muscles, tendons, ligaments, nerves, joints or spinal discs. The ones public works crews see most are:

- **Sprains** (stretched or torn ligaments) and **strains** (stretched or torn muscles or tendons), usually in the lower back, shoulders and knees.
- **Back injuries**, from a pulled muscle to a herniated disc pressing on a nerve.
- **Tendinitis**, an inflamed tendon from repeated use, common in the shoulder, elbow and wrist.
- **Carpal tunnel syndrome**, pressure on the nerve in the wrist that causes numbness, tingling and a weak grip.
- Rotator cuff tears, hernias and knee damage from kneeling.

Some MSDs happen in one moment, like a bad lift of a manhole cover. Most build up over months of small overloads until a tendon or disc gives way on an ordinary task. MSDs are among the most common and most costly injuries in public works: lost time, lost strength and sometimes a career for the worker, and overtime, light duty and claims for the department.

sections.heading: Why this training matters
sections.body:
Nearly every public works job loads the body hard. Line crews handle crossarms, transformers and reels. Water crews lift valve box lids and pull meters from pits. Collection crews lift manhole covers and drag hose. Streets crews shovel asphalt and run breakers. Refuse crews step off a truck hundreds of times a shift and tip carts that weigh more than they do. Plow and sweeper operators sit through twelve-hour routes. Operators and dispatchers hold one posture for hours.

None of that is going away. What this training changes is how you do it. A back injury does not announce itself, and the day it happens is usually not the day it started. Planning the lift, getting close, keeping the back neutral, using the cart, adjusting the seat and reporting the ache early are what keep a 30-year career from ending at year 15.

sections.heading: Risk factors and how they stack up
sections.body:
Seven risk factors drive MSDs. Each one alone raises the odds. Combined, and held long enough, they multiply.

- **Force.** Heavy lifting, pushing, pulling, carrying and hard gripping.
- **Repetition.** The same motion over and over with little recovery: lifting bags, setting cones, pulling hose.
- **Awkward posture.** Bending, reaching overhead, twisting, kneeling, working with the wrist bent or the arm out from the body.
- **Static posture.** Holding one position for a long time: crouching in a trench, holding a tool overhead, sitting through a plow route.
- **Vibration.** Hand-arm vibration from jackhammers, chainsaws, tampers and mowers; whole-body vibration from trucks, loaders and mowers.
- **Contact stress.** A hard edge pressing into soft tissue: a shovel handle in the palm, a knee on concrete.
- **Cold.** Cold cuts blood flow and grip strength, so the same task takes more force, and numb hands hide the warning signs.

Duration and recovery decide the damage. One 40-pound bag is work. Three hundred of them in a shift with a twist each time is an injury waiting for a date. Look at every task for which factors are present and which one you can remove.

sections.heading: What OSHA requires and what NIOSH recommends
sections.body:
OSHA has **no specific ergonomics standard**. It enforces ergonomic hazards under the **General Duty Clause, Section 5(a)(1) of the OSH Act**, which requires every employer to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious physical harm. In practice that means a recognized hazard causing serious injuries with a feasible fix the employer did not use, such as repeated back injuries on a task where a cart or hoist was available.

The practical guidance comes from the **NIOSH lifting equation**. It sets **51 pounds** as the maximum recommended weight for a two-handed lift under **ideal conditions**: load held close to the body at about waist height, lifted a short distance, no twisting, good handles, only occasional lifts. Every departure from ideal cuts that number. Hold the load 20 inches out from the body instead of 10 and the limit drops by half. Lifting from the floor, twisting or repeating it all morning cuts it further, and in a trench or a truck bed the recommended limit can fall below 20 pounds.

The department's rule is simple: **above about 50 pounds, or any load that is awkward, unbalanced or far from the body, get help or get equipment.**

sections.heading: Safe lifting, team lifts and mechanical aids
sections.body:
**Lifting by hand.**

1. **Plan the lift.** Clear the path, check the footing and know where the load will be set down.
2. **Test the load.** Tip a corner or lift one edge to judge weight and balance before committing.
3. **Get close.** Load against the body, feet shoulder width apart, one foot slightly ahead for a stable base.
4. **Bend the knees and hips and keep the back neutral.** Natural curve, chin up, core tight.
5. **Lift with the legs**, smoothly, no jerk. Keep the load close at waist height.
6. **Do not twist.** Move your feet to turn. Twisting under load is how discs tear.
7. **Set it down the same way**, knees and hips, load close, fingers out of the pinch.

**Team lifts.** Two people and one load need one leader. Agree on the path, the grip and the commands before anyone bends. Lift and lower on the count, match pace, and say so out loud before shifting a grip.

**Mechanical aids.** The best lift is the one you do not make. Use:

- **Hand trucks, dollies and carts** for anything that moves more than a few steps.
- **Hoists, cranes, lift gates and the digger derrick** for motors, pumps, transformers, reels and poles.
- **Manhole cover lifters**, magnetic or hook and lever, for every cover. A cover often weighs more than 100 pounds and sits at the worst height for a lift.
- **Cone placers and retrievers** for lane closures.
- **Drum handlers and pallet jacks**.
- **Pole dollies, pole jacks and pole trailers**, never shoulders alone.

If the aid is back at the shop, go get it.

sections.heading: Tools, vibration, vehicles and equipment
sections.body:
**Tools.** Pick the tool that keeps the wrist straight, the grip relaxed and the elbow near the body. A **powered tool** does the work a muscle used to, so use the impact wrench, the powered cover lifter and the hydraulic breaker when the department has them.

**Vibration.** Jackhammers, breakers, tampers, chainsaws and mowers send vibration into the hands and arms. Over time that causes **hand-arm vibration syndrome**: numb white fingers, lost grip and pain in the cold. Controls, in order: use the lowest vibration tool that does the job and keep its anti-vibration mounts in good shape; let the tool's weight do the work instead of pushing or squeezing; take breaks and rotate operators; keep hands warm and dry; and wear **anti-vibration gloves** that meet ANSI S2.73 as a supplement, not a substitute.

**Vehicles and equipment.** Adjust the seat before you move: hips to the back of the seat, knees slightly lower than hips, pedals reached without stretching, lumbar support against the low back, mirrors set so you do not twist. On long plow, sweeper and refuse routes, get out every couple of hours, walk and stretch. **Mount and dismount facing the vehicle with three points of contact**, two hands and a foot or two feet and a hand. **Never jump from a cab, step or truck bed.** A jump multiplies the load on knees and spine, and ice or a pothole turns it into a broken ankle.

sections.heading: Shoveling, refuse routes, control rooms and reporting early
sections.body:
**Shoveling and snow.** Use a shovel that fits you, with a smaller blade for wet snow and asphalt. Push snow instead of lifting when you can. Take small bites, keep the loaded blade close, and **move your feet to face where the snow goes**; never throw over the shoulder or to the side with a twist. Cold air plus heavy shoveling strains the heart, so warm up, take breaks and speak up about chest pressure or dizziness.

**Refuse collection and carts.** **Push carts instead of pulling**, with both hands. Use the truck's cart tipper every time it is available; never lift a full cart to the hopper by hand. Lift bags and cans close and do not throw them over the hopper rim with a twist. Alternate sides and switch tasks with your partner through the route.

**Office and control room.** For operators, dispatchers and office staff, static posture is the hazard. Set the **top of the monitor at or slightly below eye level**, an arm's length away and straight ahead. Set the chair so feet are flat, the low back is supported and wrists are straight. Change position every 20 to 30 minutes and take a **microbreak** of a minute or two each hour to stand, walk and look at something far away.

**Report early.** MSDs give warning: aching, stiffness, tingling, numbness, swelling, a weak grip, pain that is still there the next morning. Report it to your supervisor when it starts. Early reporting usually means a task change or a different tool; late reporting means surgery and months away. Reporting is required and protected; the department may not discourage it.

**Warm up, rotate, recover.** Take a few minutes of easy movement before heavy work; warm muscles handle load better. Rotate between tasks that load different parts of the body and build recovery into the day.

sections.heading: What this means on the job
sections.body:
**Electric Services.** Crossarms, insulators, reels, transformers and meters are heavy, awkward or both. Use the digger derrick, the bucket truck jib and the reel trailer, and plan two-person carries for anything over about 50 pounds. Meter technicians lift pit lids with the lifter, not fingers under the edge.

**Environmental Services.** Manhole covers, valve box lids, hose, sample jugs, chemical drums and pumps make up a workday of lifts. Cover lifters, drum handlers and the plant hoists are not optional. Jet and vactor crews rotate hose handling. Refuse crews push carts, use the tipper, alternate sides and never jump from the step.

**Public Services.** Streets crews shovel asphalt in small bites close to the body and use the cone placer for every closure. Forestry rotates saw operators and keeps chains sharp. Fleet mechanics use the hoist, creeper and transmission jack instead of holding parts overhead. Plow operators set the seat before the route and get out every couple of hours.

A strain that took one lift to cause can take a year to heal. Get close, keep it neutral, do not twist, and get the cart.

key_takeaways: Musculoskeletal disorders such as sprains, strains, back injuries, tendinitis and carpal tunnel syndrome are among the most common and most costly injuries in public works, and most build up over time.
Force, repetition, awkward posture, static posture, vibration, contact stress and cold are the risk factors, and the risk multiplies when several are present for long periods.
OSHA enforces ergonomic hazards under the General Duty Clause, and the NIOSH 51-pound limit applies only to ideal conditions; real limits are often far lower.
Plan the lift, test the load, get close, keep a wide base, lift with the legs and a neutral back, do not twist, and set it down the same way.
Above about 50 pounds, or for any awkward or unbalanced load, use a team lift or a mechanical aid such as a cart, hoist, lift gate, cover lifter or cone placer.
Choose tools that keep the wrist straight, control vibration at the tool and with breaks and rotation, and wear anti-vibration gloves as a supplement.
Set the seat before you drive, take breaks on long routes, mount and dismount facing the vehicle with three points of contact, and never jump from a cab or truck bed.
Report aches, tingling and numbness early, warm up before heavy work, take microbreaks and rotate tasks.

questions.text: Which of these is a musculoskeletal disorder?
options: Carbon monoxide poisoning from a running engine in the shop
A laceration from a utility knife
Tendinitis in the shoulder from months of overhead work
Hearing loss from years around a jackhammer
questions.explanation: Musculoskeletal disorders are injuries to muscles, tendons, ligaments, nerves, joints and spinal discs, such as sprains, strains, back injuries, tendinitis and carpal tunnel syndrome. Tendinitis from repeated overhead work is a classic MSD; the other choices are different kinds of injury.

questions.text: A collection crew member lifts 40-pound bags from the ground, twisting to toss each one into the hopper, about 300 times a shift in January. Which statement is correct?
options: Force, repetition, awkward posture and cold are all present, and together they raise the risk far more than any one of them alone
The task is acceptable because each bag is under the 51-pound NIOSH limit
Only the twisting counts as a risk factor, since 40 pounds is a light load
Cold weather lowers the risk because muscles work harder and stay warm
questions.explanation: Risk factors stack. Force, repetition, the awkward twisting posture and cold are each present, and the duration across a full shift multiplies the exposure. The 51-pound NIOSH figure applies only to ideal conditions and drops sharply with twisting, floor-level lifts and frequent repetition.

questions.text: Under what authority does OSHA cite an employer for an ergonomic hazard?
options: 29 CFR 1910.900, the ergonomics program standard
The General Duty Clause, Section 5(a)(1) of the OSH Act
29 CFR 1926.1053, which sets lifting limits for construction
OSHA cannot cite ergonomic hazards because there is no standard
questions.explanation: OSHA has no specific ergonomics standard in force, so it enforces recognized ergonomic hazards under the General Duty Clause, which requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm when a feasible fix exists.

questions.text: The NIOSH lifting equation sets 51 pounds as the maximum recommended weight. Under what conditions does that number apply?
options: Any two-handed lift by a worker in good physical condition
Lifts from the floor to shoulder height with a firm grip
Team lifts, with each person's share counted separately
Ideal conditions only: load close to the body at about waist height, short lift distance, no twisting, good handles and only occasional lifting
questions.explanation: The 51-pound figure is the load constant for ideal conditions. The equation reduces it for horizontal distance from the body, lifting from low or high positions, long vertical travel, twisting, frequency and poor grip, so real-world limits are usually much lower.

questions.text: You have lifted a pump off a pallet and need to set it on a cart to your left. What is the correct move?
options: Move your feet to turn your whole body toward the cart, keep the load close and lower with your legs
Rotate at the waist while holding the pump at arm's length so you can see the cart
Rest the pump on your knee, then swing it onto the cart
Lean over the cart and drop the pump the last few inches to save your back
questions.explanation: Twisting under load is one of the main ways spinal discs are injured. Turning with the feet keeps the spine neutral, keeping the load close reduces the force on the back, and lowering with the legs sets the load down the same way it was lifted.

questions.text: Two workers need to carry an 80-pound motor across the shop. What makes the team lift safe?
options: Each person lifts their end as soon as they are ready, so neither waits with a load
The stronger worker takes most of the weight so the other can steer
One person leads, they agree on the path, grip and commands before bending, and they lift, move and lower on the count
They carry it at arm's length so they can see their feet
questions.explanation: A team lift needs one leader, an agreed path and commands, and lifting and lowering on the count so the load does not shift to one person. The load stays close to both bodies, and anyone who needs to adjust says so out loud first.

questions.text: A 24-inch manhole cover needs to come off for a sewer inspection. What is the right way to lift it?
options: Pry up one edge with a screwdriver and slide fingers underneath to flip it
Use a magnetic or hook-and-lever manhole cover lifter and keep the back neutral
Have one worker stand on the far edge while another pulls up the near edge
Loop a chain through the pick hole and lift it straight up by hand
questions.explanation: A manhole cover often weighs more than 100 pounds and sits at ground level far from the feet, the worst possible lifting position. The department's cover lifters are the mechanical aid for that job, and fingers never go under a cover's edge.

questions.text: A streets crew member runs a jackhammer for most of a shift. Which control reduces hand-arm vibration exposure the most?
options: Gripping the handles harder so the tool stays steady
Wearing two pairs of ordinary leather gloves
Leaning body weight onto the tool to break the pavement faster
Using a lower vibration tool with working anti-vibration mounts, letting the tool's weight do the work, rotating operators and keeping hands warm
questions.explanation: The controls that reduce vibration exposure are a lower vibration tool in good repair, a relaxed grip that lets the tool work, breaks and operator rotation, warm hands and anti-vibration gloves that meet ANSI S2.73. Gripping harder and leaning in increase the vibration that reaches the hands.

questions.text: A plow operator finishes a 12-hour route and needs to get out of the cab. What is the correct dismount?
options: Face the cab, keep three points of contact on the steps and grab handles and step down to the ground
Turn to face outward and jump down so both feet land at once
Face outward and walk down the steps like a staircase while holding the door
Slide out of the seat onto the top step and hop to the ground
questions.explanation: Mounting and dismounting facing the vehicle with three points of contact keeps you in control on steps that may be icy or muddy. Jumping or hopping from a cab or truck bed multiplies the load on the knees and spine and is a common cause of ankle, knee and back injuries.

questions.text: A water plant operator notices tingling and numbness in her hand at the end of most shifts. What should she do?
options: Wait to see if it goes away over the winter before saying anything
Switch to using the other hand and keep it to herself so it is not held against her
Report it to her supervisor now so the task, tool or workstation can be changed before it becomes a lasting injury
Report it only after it keeps her from working a full shift
questions.explanation: Tingling and numbness are early warning signs of an MSD such as carpal tunnel syndrome. Early reporting usually leads to a task change, a different tool or a workstation adjustment; waiting lets the injury progress until it needs surgery and time away. Employees may not be discouraged from reporting.
